title: The Golden Bough: A Study in Magic and Religion
author: Sir James George Frazer
edition_analyzed: 1922 Abridged Edition (most common for modern readers, edited by Frazer himself)
target_audience: Scholars of anthropology, religion, and folklore
University students in the humanities and social sciences
General readers interested in myths, ritual, and comparative religion
Writers, artists, and cultural critics seeking insights into universal mythic patterns
core_themes: Universality of myth and ritual across cultures
Transition from magical to religious to scientific modes of thinking
The concept of the dying and reviving god
Cycles of nature and human society
primary_purpose: To systematically study and compare the myths, rituals, and religious practices of different cultures worldwide, arguing for common underlying patterns and the progression of human thought from magic through religion to science.

structure_format.narrative_style: Scholarly, discursive, and richly detailed with citations and references
structure_format.organization: Organized into chapters by thematic topics (e.g., magical rites, taboo, the scapegoat, vegetation gods, kingship), with cross-cultural examples and comparative analysis
features: Extensive use of ethnographic examples from diverse societies
Footnotes and references to classical and contemporary sources
Reflective commentary and synthesis drawing general principles from specific cases

key_concepts_lessons: Many ancient religious and mythic customs share common features, regardless of region or ethnicity.
Magic, religion, and science represent successive ways humans have attempted to understand and control the world.
The ritual killing of kings or priests as fertility rites is a recurring theme in global mythology.
The dying and resurrecting god motif underpins myths from Adonis and Osiris to Christian narratives.
Taboos, sacrifices, and festivals serve as mechanisms for managing fear, uncertainty, and social cohesion.
Superstitions and rituals often stem from attempts to influence nature through imitative or sympathetic magic.
style_tone: Objective (at times Victorian in style and assumptions)
Analytical but also imaginative and evocative
notable_features: Monumental compendium of mythological, ethnographic, and folk beliefs
Introduced and popularized comparative mythology as a scholarly approach
Influenced generations of writers, psychologists, and artists (e.g., T.S. Eliot, Joseph Campbell, Sigmund Freud)
Abridged and unabridged versions available; the abridged 1922 edition is most accessible for lay readers
cultural_historical_context: Written during the late 19th and early 20th centuries—a period of expanding interest in global anthropology, colonial ethnography, and comparative mythology. Frazer drew from Victorian and Edwardian intellectual currents and burgeoning academic fields, shaping Western understanding of myth and ritual.
reception_impact: Seminal influence in anthropology, folklore, and mythological studies throughout the 20th century
Praised for its breadth and imaginative synthesis
Subject to critique for Eurocentric, sometimes speculative conclusions, and lack of fieldwork
Inspired major literary and artistic works, shaping ideas about mythic archetypes
Some theories (e.g., the centrality of the dying god) have been challenged or revised by later scholarship
